summary: Clarifies how to use the PIDF-LO location format, which can represent location in many ways. When systems must constrain that flexibility, the many options become a problem, so this document gives recommendations for representing location consistently.

plainLanguage.summary: A location format can describe a place in many ways, like giving an address or map coordinates. This note says which ways to choose so different systems understand each other.

questions: how to represent location in geopriv
how many points can a pidf-lo polygon have
which geodetic shapes must pidf-lo support
which location wins in a pidf-lo with several locations
subtitle: Nine rules and a shape profile that make a PIDF-LO location unambiguous enough to route on.

tldr.problem: A PIDF-LO document can hold any number of location objects, some contradictory, and RFC 4119's geodetic examples use a deprecated, opaque coordinate format. Software that routes on location cannot tell which one to trust.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets nine rules for building and reading a PIDF-LO that conveys one location, and makes the eight GeoShape shapes mandatory, with fixed coordinate reference systems, units and polygon limits.
tldr.outcome: Creators and consumers of location can interpret the same document the same way. The RFC updates RFC 4119 and has itself been updated by RFC 7459.

today: RFC 5491 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4119, and it has been updated by RFC 7459. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why PIDF-LO Needs Constraining
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO, RFC 4119) is the recommended way of encoding location information and its privacy policies. Location may be geospatial, using a subset of Geography Markup Language (GML) 3.1.1, or civic, as in RFC 5139.

That flexibility is deliberate, and this RFC does not forbid it. What it adds is a set of guidelines for the cases where it is important to unambiguously convey exactly one location, such as location-based routing. The key words MUST and SHOULD carry their RFC 2119 meaning.

The RFC also defines a few terms. A discrete location is a place, point, area or volume in which a Target can be found. A compound location combines civic and geodetic information, for example a polygon for a building plus a civic element for the floor.
sections.plainLanguage: A location note is allowed to say many things. When a computer has to pick one answer, it needs a few simple rules about how the note is written.

sections.title: Where Locations Live in a Document
sections.content:
A presence document may contain any number of <tuple>, <device> and <person> elements. Each holds a <status> element that may contain more than one <geopriv> element. Each <geopriv> must contain a <location-info> element and a <usage-rules> element, and <location-info> holds one or more location elements.

So a single document can carry an arbitrary number of locations, some contradictory and some complementary. The RFC says this leads to confusion for the generators, conveyors and consumers of location, and that practical experience in the US National Emergency Number Association (NENA) produced the conventions that follow.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a folder with many pockets, and every pocket can hold a note saying where someone is. The notes might disagree, so you need to know which pocket to read first.

sections.title: The Nine Rules
sections.content:
The rules have no particular order. Creators and consumers should follow them so the data is interpreted consistently.

  • Rule 1: a <geopriv> element MUST describe a discrete location.
  • Rule 2: if a location can be described in more than one way, each description SHOULD sit in its own <tuple>, <device> or <person>, with one geopriv element per tuple.
  • Rule 3: more than one <geopriv> in a document MUST only be used if the locations refer to the same place or are in different element types.
  • Rules 4 to 6: avoid several location chunks in one <location-info>. If you do, they MUST come from a common source at the same time by the same method, and SHOULD only form a compound location for the same place.
  • Rule 7: in a compound location, the coarse information MUST come first, for example the area before the floor.
  • Rule 8: with several geopriv elements, priority goes to the first <device> that has a location, then the first <tuple>. Locations in <person> SHOULD only be a last resort.
  • Rule 9: when several documents arrive together, such as in a multi-part MIME body, selection SHOULD follow document order, first document first.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: one note, one place. If you must put several, put the most general first, and readers should start with the device's note, then the others, and the first one in the pile.

sections.title: The Rules in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC walks through four scenarios. In the first, a laptop on a coffee shop's WiFi gets a civic address, perhaps via DHCP (RFC 4776), and a single tuple or device with one geopriv and one location chunk is unambiguous.

In the second, a laptop on an office Ethernet port gets a geodetic point plus a civic element giving the floor. Rules 6 and 7 produce a compound location with the point first and the floor second.

In the third, a laptop carrying a stored home address visits another city and receives a new location from the visited network. The system cannot tell whether the two describe the same place, so it generates a new PIDF-LO. If the new location were added to the old document anyway, breaking rule 3, rules 8 and 9 still help: put the new one first, in a separate tuple.

In the fourth, a PC is misconfigured and reports the office while its owner is in the park. The document holds a <device> location and a different <person> location, which is allowed because they are different element types.
sections.plainLanguage: If you travel with an old address saved, you write a fresh note for the new place and put it on top. If your laptop and you are in different places, you write one note for each.

sections.title: Geodetic Shapes and Coordinates
sections.content:
The geodetic examples in RFC 4119 use the <gml:location> element with <gml:coordinates> inside <gml:Point>. The RFC lists two drawbacks: it is deprecated from GML 3.1 onward, and the coordinates format is opaque, so the same location can be written many ways.

Instead, the GeoShape specification gives a GML profile for common shapes, and the shapes it defines are the recommended ones. It defines eight, and they MUST be implemented:

  • Point (2d and 3d)
  • Polygon (2d)
  • Circle (2d)
  • Ellipse (2d)
  • Arc band (2d)
  • Sphere (3d)
  • Ellipsoid (3d)
  • Prism (3d)

The RFC notes that cellular systems usually express location as a point plus an area or volume of uncertainty, but in practice most systems use the point as an absolute value and ignore the uncertainty.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a confusing string of numbers, everyone agrees on eight simple shapes, like a dot, a circle or a box, to draw where something is.

sections.title: Coordinate Systems, Units and Polygon Limits
sections.content:
The RFC mandates WGS84 with EPSG code 4326 (urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4326) for 2d shapes and EPSG 4979 (urn:ogc:def:crs:EPSG::4979) for 3d volumes. Distances and heights are in meters, using urn:ogc:def:uom:EPSG::9001. Angles MUST use degrees (urn:ogc:def:uom:EPSG::9102) or radians (urn:ogc:def:uom:EPSG::9101), and bearings run clockwise from true north, not magnetic north.

Implementations MUST give the coordinate reference system in the srsName attribute of the outermost geometry element, and MUST NOT respecify it for sub-elements. The srsDimension attribute SHOULD be omitted. User-defined systems need not be supported. It is RECOMMENDED that uncertainty be expressed at a confidence of 95% or higher.

For polygons, the GeoShape spec sets no limit on vertices, but arbitrarily complex shapes could hurt real-time processing such as routing. So polygons SHOULD have at most 15 points (16 with the repeated point), matching limits in 3GPP and OMA. Adjacent vertices SHOULD be at most 130 km apart, edges must not cross, and vertices MUST run counter-clockwise so the upward normal points up. In 3d, all points MUST share one altitude.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must use the same globe, the same ruler (meters) and the same way of measuring turns. Shapes with a million corners are discouraged, since a computer in a hurry would struggle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the primary security considerations relate to how location information is conveyed and used, which are outside its scope. It is meant only as guidelines on which elements MUST or SHOULD be implemented by systems doing location-dependent routing, and those recommendations extend to the devices and clients that use such services.
sections.plainLanguage: This note only tells you how to write the location down. How to keep it safe on the way is somebody else's job.
